## Introduction

In these exercises, you'll practice with everything from this week:
finding your way around OSC OnDemand, working in VS Code,
writing Markdown, and organizing and documenting a research project.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
#### No Unix shell needed
You haven't learned the Unix shell yet --- that starts next week.
Everything below can be done with the OnDemand file browser,
the VS Code interface, and your keyboard.
So don't worry if you see a terminal in VS Code: leave it alone for now.
:::

You'll write a separate file for each exercise,
which should all go in a folder `week02/exercises` inside your personal dir
at `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>`:

| Exercise                                | File you will create               | Time    |
| --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------- |
| 1 --- Getting comfortable in VS Code    | `vscode.md`                        | ~10 min |
| 2 --- Finding your way around OSC       | `osc.md`                           | ~15 min |
| 3 --- Writing a Markdown document       | `markdown-practice.md`             | ~20 min |
| 4 --- Fixing a broken Markdown file     | `broken.md`                        | ~15 min |
| 5 --- File names and project structure  | `file-names.md` + a project folder | ~25 min |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[42,40,18]"}

### Setting up

1. Start a VS Code (`Code Server`) session at OSC OnDemand,
   as described in [the VS Code lecture](./w2c_vscode.qmd#starting-vs-code-at-osc).
   Make sure the **Working Directory** is your personal dir,
   `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>`.

2. When VS Code has opened,
   the file explorer in the Primary Side Bar should show the `week02` and
   `week03` folders you created in class.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Solutions for most questions are at the [bottom of this page](#solutions) ---
but do give each question a genuine try before looking!
:::

## Exercise 1: Getting comfortable in VS Code

_Write your answers in a file `vscode.md`, which you'll create in step 2._

1. In the file explorer, hover your mouse over the `week02` folder:
   a couple of small icons will appear to the right of the folder name.
   Click the "New Folder..." icon
   (the one that looks like a folder with a `+`) and create a folder
   called `exercises`.

2. Now hover over your new `exercises` folder and click the "New File..." icon
   to create a file called `vscode.md`.
   Because you created it directly in the file explorer,
   you don't have to save it in the right place afterwards.

3. Type a level-1 header `# VS Code notes` on the first line of the file,
   and a short sentence below it.
   _(You'll add the answers to the questions below to this file, too.)_

4. Open a live preview of the file by clicking the preview icon in the
   top-right of the editor pane.
   Then close the preview tab again.

5. Open the Command Palette
   ({{< fa cog >}} > `Command Palette`),
   type `markdown preview`, and use it to open the preview to the side again.
   In the Command Palette, a keyboard shortcut is listed to the right of
   the command --- note that shortcut in your file.

6. With the preview open, type a few more words in your file.
   Do you need to save the file for the preview to update?
   Note the answer in your file.

7. Open the settings ({{< fa cog >}} > `Settings`),
   type `word wrap` in the search box, and set `Editor: Word Wrap` to `on`.
   Type (or paste) a very long line in your file and note in your file
   what this setting changed.

8. If you didn't already do so in class, change your color theme
   ({{< fa cog >}} > `Themes` > `Color Theme`),
   and note in your file which theme you picked.

9. Open a terminal ({{< fa bars >}} > `Terminal` > `New Terminal`)
   and then close the whole panel again by clicking the `X` in its top-right
   corner. _(Don't type anything in the terminal --- that's for next week!)_

## Exercise 2: Finding your way around OSC

_Write your answers in a file `osc.md` in your `week02/exercises` folder._
_Create it in VS Code just like you did in the previous exercise, and_
_number your answers to match the questions._

For this exercise, open OnDemand (<https://ondemand.osc.edu>) in a
**second browser tab**, so you can keep your VS Code session open in the first.

1. In the `Files` dropdown menu, click `Home Directory`.
   The full path of the folder you're in is shown at the top of the page:
   put it in your file, formatted as inline code.

2. Your Home dir path contains a project number.
   Does that mean your Home dir belongs to that project?
   Answer in one sentence.

3. In the `Files` menu, click `/fs/ess/PAS3493` and navigate into the
   `people` folder and then into your own folder.
   Click the "Copy path" button at the top of the page,
   and paste the path into your file as inline code.

4. How many folders does `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people` contain,
   and what do those folders represent?

5. From within your personal folder, navigate into `week02` and then
   `exercises`. Do you see the files you made in VS Code?
   In one sentence, explain why (or why not).

6. In the `Files` menu, go to the **scratch** folder for our project.
   Put its full path in your file,
   and name one type of file that you would store there rather than in
   `/fs/ess/PAS3493`.

7. In the `Clusters` menu, click `System Status`.
   Which of the three clusters currently has the largest percentage of its
   nodes in use, and how many nodes does Cardinal have in total?

8. In the `Jobs` menu, click `Active Jobs` and find your own VS Code job.
   Which cluster is it running on, and what is the name of the node
   it was assigned?

9. Is the VS Code session you are working in running on a login node or on a
   compute node? Explain your answer in one sentence.

10. For each of the following, say whether you would store it in
    **Home**, **Project** (`/fs/ess`), or **Scratch** --- and why:

    a. 300 GB of alignment (BAM) files that you can regenerate from your raw
       data, and that you'll be done with in two weeks.
    b. The raw sequence data for your lab's newest experiment.
    c. A set of small utility scripts that you personally reuse across all the
       projects you work on.

## Exercise 3: Writing a Markdown document

In this exercise, you'll build a Markdown document from scratch.
The idea is to practice the *syntax*, so don't spend much time thinking about
the content --- a few words per item is plenty.

1. Create a new file `markdown-practice.md` in your `week02/exercises` folder,
   and open a preview to the side.
   **Keep an eye on the preview after every step below.**

2. On the first line, add a level-1 header with the document's title:
   `Markdown practice`.

3. Add a level-2 header `Course tools`,
   and below it a paragraph of two sentences about the tools you've used
   so far in this course.

4. Below that paragraph, add a bulleted list with three tools.
   For each item, put the name of the tool in **bold**,
   followed by a dash and a few words about what it's used for.

5. Add a level-2 header `Starting a VS Code session at OSC`,
   and below it a numbered list of four steps.
   Number *every* item `1.` in the source, and check what the preview does
   with the numbers.

6. Add a level-2 header `Useful links` with a bulleted list of two links:

   - A link to <https://www.markdownguide.org> whose link text is
     `The Markdown Guide` (so the URL itself is not visible).
   - A link to the OnDemand portal that *does* show the URL.

7. Add a level-2 header `A quote`,
   and below it a blockquote with one sentence that you found interesting from
   this week's reading [@markowetz2015].
   Below the blockquote, in a regular paragraph, say where the quote is from.

8. Add a level-2 header `Code`, and below it:

   - A sentence that mentions the file name `README.md`,
     formatted as inline code.
   - A code block with `bash` syntax highlighting containing these two lines:

     ```bash
     # Print the current date and time
     date
     ```

9. Add a horizontal rule, followed by a level-2 header `To do`
   and a bulleted list of two things you want to practice more.
   Then indent the second item by four spaces and check the preview:
   what happened?
   Add a sentence to your document describing what you see.

10. Finally, delete the blank line between one of your paragraphs and the list
    that follows it, and look at the preview.
    Then put the blank line back.

## Solutions

### Exercise 1

<details><summary>**5.** The keyboard shortcut for the Markdown preview</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The Command Palette lists <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>K</kbd> followed by
<kbd>V</kbd> for `Markdown: Open Preview to the Side`
(and <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>V</kbd> for a full-window preview).

Note that browser and operating system shortcuts can "shadow" VS Code
shortcuts when you use VS Code inside a browser like this,
so not every shortcut you see listed will actually work at OSC.

</details>

<details><summary>**6.** Does the preview update without saving?</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

No --- the preview updates as you type, without you having to save.
That said, you should still save your file regularly:
the preview shows your unsaved changes, but nothing else does.

</details>

<details><summary>**7.** What does the "word wrap" setting do?</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

With word wrap off (the default),
a long line runs off the right edge of the editor and you have to scroll
sideways to read it.
With word wrap on, the line is displayed across multiple lines in the editor.

Importantly, this only changes the *display*: no line breaks are added to
the file itself, so the rendered output is unaffected.

</details>

### Exercise 2

<details><summary>**1.-2.** Your Home dir and the project number in its path</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Your Home dir path has the form `/users/<project>/<user>` ---
for example, `/users/PAS0471/jelmer`.

The project number in that path is merely the project that your OSC account
was created under, and your Home dir is not meaningfully associated with it:
it is *your personal* storage space.
Recall that you have exactly one Home dir,
no matter how many projects you are a member of.

</details>

<details><summary>**3.-5.** Your personal folder in the project storage</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Your personal folder for this course is
`/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>`,
where `<user>` is your OSC username.

The `people` folder contains one folder for each student in the course that
has created their personal folder --- so the number will grow over the
first weeks of the course.

And yes, you should see the files you created in VS Code:
the OnDemand file browser and VS Code are two different windows onto the
*same* file system at OSC.
Which one you use to create a folder or file makes no difference.

</details>

<details><summary>**6.** The scratch folder</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The scratch folder for our project is `/fs/scratch/PAS3493`.

Good candidates for scratch storage are large files that you can regenerate,
and that you don't need for long ---
for example, intermediate files produced halfway through an analysis.
Files in scratch storage are automatically deleted after a number of days,
so never put anything there that you can't recreate.

</details>

<details><summary>**7.-9.** System status, your job, and login vs. compute nodes</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The answers to the first two questions depend on when you look:
cluster usage changes by the minute,
and which node you were assigned differs among students and among sessions.
Cardinal has 378 nodes.

Your VS Code session runs on a **compute node**.
That's exactly why you had to fill out a form with a cluster, a project to
bill, and a number of hours when you started it:
you were requesting a compute job, and the job scheduler reserved a compute
node for you.
You can see this on the `Active Jobs` page,
where your session is listed as a job with a specific node assigned to it.

</details>

<details><summary>**10.** Which storage area?</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

a. **Scratch** --- large, regenerable, and short-lived: a textbook case for
   scratch storage.
b. **Project** (`/fs/ess`) --- raw data belonging to a lab's project,
   which should be stored (and backed up) with that project.
c. **Home** --- these are personal files that are not tied to any one project.

</details>

### Exercise 4

<details><summary>The ten problems, and the fixed file</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The problems were:

1. No space after the `#` of the title, so it isn't a header.
2. No blank line between the paragraph and the list below it,
   so the list isn't rendered as a list.
3. No space after the `-` of the second list item.
4. "I started a VS Code session at OSC." and "Then I opened a Markdown file."
   are on separate lines in the source but end up in one line in the output:
   a single line break is ignored.
5. The link has its two parts reversed:
   the `[link text]` comes first, and then the `(URL)`.
6. The inline code for `notes.md` has an opening backtick but no closing one.
7. `**really*` has two asterisks on one side and one on the other,
   so no formatting is applied.
8. No blank line before the `## Things to try next week` header.
9. The `bash`/`date` code block lost its triple backticks.
10. The table is missing the row of dashes below the header row,
    so it isn't rendered as a table.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

And here is the fixed file:

````markdown

The guide is [Markdown Guide](https://www.markdownguide.org).
````

end the first one with a backslash (`\`).
:::

### Exercise 5

<details><summary>**A)** Better file names</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Several other answers are possible ---
what matters is that your names are machine-readable, human-readable,
and sort correctly.

1. `Final Results May 3 2016 (2).xlsx` &rarr; `results_2016-05-03.xlsx`\
   Spaces and parentheses aren't machine-readable,
   `May 3 2016` doesn't sort correctly,
   and "Final" and "(2)" say nothing about the contents.
   _(And ideally, this wouldn't be an `.xlsx` file at all.)_

2. `sample2_R1.fastq` &rarr; `sample02_R1.fastq`\
   Without a leading zero, `sample10` sorts before `sample2`.
   With 40 samples, two digits are enough.

3. `RNAseq counts FINAL.csv` &rarr; `rnaseq_counts.csv`\
   No spaces, no capitals, and "FINAL" is what version control is for.

4. `DNA extraction protocol v2.docx` &rarr; `dna-extraction-protocol.md`\
   No spaces; hyphens separate the words within one unit.
   A protocol is a great candidate for a plain-text (Markdown) file,
   and again, `v2` is better handled with version control.

5. `plot1.png` &rarr; `pca_all-samples.png`\
   The original is machine-readable but not human-readable:
   it says nothing about what the figure shows.

6. `2019_3_7_field_notes.txt` &rarr; `field-notes_2019-03-07.txt`\
   The date needs leading zeros and hyphens to sort correctly,
   and underscores are better reserved for separating units
   (here: the date from the description).

</details>

<details><summary>**B)** Where the files of the fictional project go</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

```bash-out-solo
rnaseq-treatment/
|-- README.md
|-- data/
|   |-- meta/
|   |   |-- samples.tsv
|   |-- raw/
|   |   |-- ctrl01_R1.fastq.gz
|   |   |-- ctrl01_R2.fastq.gz
|   |   |-- treated10_R1.fastq.gz
|   |-- ref/
|   |   |-- GCF_016801865.2.fna
|-- doc/
|   |-- diary.md
|-- results/
|   |-- counts/
|   |   |-- counts.csv
|   |-- figures/
|   |   |-- pca_all-samples.png
|-- scripts/
|   |-- 01_align-reads.sh
|   |-- 02_plot-counts.R
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Some things to note:

- The sample sheet is *metadata* --- data about your samples --- so it belongs
  in `data`, and it should be converted from `.xlsx` to a plain-text format.
- `counts.csv` is produced by one of your scripts, which makes it a *result*,
  even though the next script uses it as input.
- The reference genome is data that you downloaded rather than generated,
  and it goes in `data` too.
- `notes 5-3-26.txt` was a lab notebook file, so it became `doc/diary.md`
  (with `## 2026-05-03` as the header of that day's entry).
- Numbering the scripts shows the order in which they should be run.

</details>

<br>
